hops.afterHeading: What the mechanism must do: a veto on the null direction
hops.title: A beetle on a spherical Y-maze
hops.text: In 1956, Bernhard Hassenstein and Werner Reichardt worked out how an insect might detect motion without recording a single neuron. Their subject was a beetle, *Chlorophanus viridis*, walking on a small spherical Y-maze while patterns moved around it. They simply tracked which way it tended to turn. From that footwork they proposed a detector that compares two neighbouring facets of the eye, delays one signal and multiplies the pair, so a sequence in the preferred direction gets a boost. Nine years later, Barlow and Levick's rabbit cells turned out to rely mainly on the opposite trick: a veto on the null direction.

sources.citation: Borst A, Haag J, Mauss AS. How fly neurons compute the direction of visual motion. J Comp Physiol A. 2020;206(2):109-124.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small green beetle held by a thin wire walks a tiny straw ball inside a black and white striped cylinder.
image.caption: From which way a walking beetle turned, Hassenstein and Reichardt proposed a motion detector that boosts the preferred direction.

hops.afterHeading: Each branch is its own detector (2002)
hops.title: Watch a friend's eyes on a train
hops.text: Next time you ride a train or bus with a friend, watch their eyes while they look out the side window. The eyes glide smoothly with the passing scenery, flick back, then glide again, in a steady sawtooth rhythm. It happens even when people simply stare at the passing scenery. This is optokinetic nystagmus, the visible beat of the optokinetic reflex, the same reflex that disappeared when Yoshida's team removed starburst cells from mice. Eye doctors use it to check vision in babies too young for an eye chart: they turn a striped drum and find the finest stripes that still pull the eyes along.

sources.citation: Turuwhenua J, et al. A Comparison of Centroid Tracking and Image Phase for Improved Optokinetic Nystagmus Detection. J Eye Mov Res. 2026;19(1):12.
Kassin-Dufresne M, Charest Bosse MC, Aron M. Optokinetic After-Nystagmus: A Marker for Migraine? J Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2025;54:19160216241307553.
Yoshida K, et al. A key role of starburst amacrine cells in originating retinal directional selectivity and optokinetic eye movement. Neuron. 2001;30(3):771-780.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two young adults by a train window, one smiling while watching the other's eyes follow the passing trees.
image.caption: Scenery sliding past a window pulls the eyes into a smooth glide and quick flick back, over and over.

hops.title: A gene that helps wire horizontal motion detection
hops.text: Idiopathic congenital nystagmus makes the eyes move involuntarily from side to side from about two or three months of age. Changes in *FRMD7*, a gene on the X chromosome, explain many inherited cases. When Keisuke Yonehara, Botond Roska and colleagues tested people with *FRMD7* changes in 2016, their optokinetic reflex was missing for horizontal motion but normal for vertical motion. Mice offered a clue. In the mouse retina, FRMD7 is made specifically in starburst cells, and in mice with a faulty copy of the gene, inhibition onto ganglion cells that normally prefer horizontal motion came out nearly symmetric instead of lopsided. Cells tuned to vertical motion kept their direction selectivity.

sources.citation: Yonehara K, et al. Congenital Nystagmus Gene FRMD7 Is Necessary for Establishing a Neuronal Circuit Asymmetry for Direction Selectivity. Neuron. 2016;89(1):177-193.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small brown mouse on a platform in the centre of a large drum lined with vertical black and white stripes.
image.caption: In mice, a gene made in starburst cells helps build the lopsided inhibition behind horizontal motion tracking.
